blurb: Peru's capital sits on cliffs above the Pacific and is the food capital of South America: ceviche at lunch, sunsets over the ocean.
fun_fact: Lima is one of the driest capitals on Earth: it gets less than 2 cm of rain a year, yet a grey sea mist, the garúa, hangs over it for months.

blurb: A desert peninsula where the sand runs into the sea, and a short boat ride to the Ballestas Islands: sea lions, Humboldt penguins and huge bird colonies.
fun_fact: On the way to the islands you pass the Candelabro, a figure about 170 m tall carved into a sandy hillside. Nobody knows for sure who made it, or when.

blurb: A tiny palm-fringed lagoon surrounded by giant sand dunes, made for dune buggies, sandboarding and sunsets from the crest.
fun_fact: For years Huacachina was printed on the back of Peru's 50-sol banknote.

blurb: The White City, built from pale volcanic stone under the snowy cone of El Misti, with one of the best colonial centres in South America.
fun_fact: The Santa Catalina Monastery is a walled town inside the town, about 20,000 m² of lanes and cloisters. It stayed closed to the outside world for almost 400 years and opened to visitors only in 1970.

blurb: A huge canyon lined with pre-Inca terraces, where Andean condors glide past the viewpoint in the early morning.
fun_fact: At about 3,270 m at its deepest, Colca is almost twice as deep as the Grand Canyon.

blurb: Peru's port on Lake Titicaca, the base for the floating reed islands of the Uros and the weaving island of Taquile.
fun_fact: The Uros islands are made of totora reeds: as the bottom layers rot in the water, the islanders keep adding fresh reeds on top.

blurb: The old Inca capital at 3,400 m: Spanish churches and balconies built straight on top of perfect Inca stone walls.
fun_fact: The Inca walls fit without any mortar. The famous Twelve-Angled Stone in Hatun Rumiyoc street locks into its neighbours on all twelve sides.

blurb: The green valley of the Urubamba river below Cusco, lined with Inca terraces, salt pans and market villages.
fun_fact: People still live in Ollantaytambo on its original Inca street plan, with stone water channels running along the lanes.

blurb: The village at the foot of Machu Picchu, reached only by train or on foot, and the start of the bus up to the citadel.
fun_fact: Machu Picchu was built around 1450 and the Spanish conquerors never found it. It became world famous only after Hiram Bingham's visit in 1911.

blurb: Tango, steak and grand boulevards: a European-looking capital on the River Plate that eats dinner at ten.
fun_fact: Avenida 9 de Julio is listed by Guinness as the widest avenue in the world: about 110 m and 16 lanes of traffic.

blurb: A small town on the turquoise Lago Argentino and the base for the Perito Moreno glacier, where towers of ice crash into the lake.
fun_fact: The town is named after the calafate bush. Local legend says that whoever eats its berries will come back to Patagonia.

blurb: Argentina's trekking capital: a village of hikers right under the granite spires of Fitz Roy and Cerro Torre.
fun_fact: El Chaltén is one of the youngest towns in Argentina: it was founded in 1985, partly to settle a border dispute with Chile.

blurb: A windy fishing town on a fjord, the base for Torres del Paine, with mountain views straight from the waterfront.
fun_fact: In a cave nearby, settlers found the skin and bones of a giant ground sloth, the mylodon. A scrap of that skin inspired Bruce Chatwin's book In Patagonia.

blurb: Granite towers, glaciers and blue lakes: one of the great treks of the world, walked in four or five days.
fun_fact: 'Paine' means 'blue' in the language of the Tehuelche people, so the name means roughly 'Towers of Blue'.

blurb: One of the southernmost cities in the world, on the Strait of Magellan, with penguin colonies a boat ride away.
fun_fact: Before the Panama Canal opened in 1914, ships between the Atlantic and the Pacific sailed past here, and the port grew rich on them.

blurb: The northernmost capital in the world: colourful houses, geothermal pools and the rocket-shaped Hallgrímskirkja church.
fun_fact: Almost every home in Reykjavík is heated with natural hot water piped in from geothermal fields.

blurb: Iceland's classic loop: the rift valley of Þingvellir, the spouting Geysir field and the double waterfall of Gullfoss.
fun_fact: At Þingvellir you walk in the rift between the North American and Eurasian plates, which move apart by about 2 cm a year.

blurb: A village on the south coast with black sand beaches, basalt columns and sea stacks rising out of the Atlantic.
fun_fact: Legend says the Reynisdrangar sea stacks are trolls who were turned to stone by the sunrise while dragging a ship to shore.

blurb: A green oasis between glacier tongues in Vatnajökull National Park, with Svartifoss, the waterfall framed by black basalt columns.
fun_fact: Vatnajökull, the ice cap above you, is the largest in Iceland and covers about 8% of the country.

blurb: Vietnam's capital: lakes, a thousand-year-old centre and street food on every pavement.
fun_fact: Old Quarter streets are named after what they used to sell: Hàng Bạc is Silver Street, Hàng Gai is Hemp Street.

names: Ha Long and Lan Ha Bay
blurb: Around 1,600 limestone islands rising out of emerald water, best seen from a boat with a night on board.
fun_fact: Ha Long means 'descending dragon': legend says the islands are jewels that dragons spat into the sea to defend the coast.

blurb: Rice fields and limestone peaks you explore by rowing boat along the river, often called Ha Long Bay on land.
fun_fact: Many of the Tam Coc boat rowers row with their feet, leaning back and pushing the oars with their legs.

blurb: The old imperial capital on the Perfume River, with a walled citadel and the royal tombs of the Nguyễn emperors.
fun_fact: Hue was the capital of Vietnam from 1802 to 1945, under the Nguyễn, the country's last royal dynasty.

blurb: A lantern-lit old trading port with yellow merchant houses, and tailors who make you clothes overnight.
fun_fact: Its Japanese Covered Bridge, from the late 16th century, is printed on Vietnam's 20,000-dong banknote.

blurb: Vietnam's biggest city, still called Saigon by most people: motorbikes, markets and rooftop bars.
fun_fact: The Cu Chi tunnels, a day trip away, once ran for more than 200 km underground during the war.
